title: Understanding Latin America’s Self-Employment
gist: Former World Bank LAC chief economist William Maloney argues Latin America's high informal self-employment is a rational, development-consistent choice driven by valued amenities rather than a pathology, so micro-firm formalization programs will disappoint; growth and formality must come from skills, a more dynamic large-firm sector, calibrated minimum wages and integrated social-protection redesign.

insights.claim: Roughly half of Latin America and the Caribbean's 325 million workers lack a formal labor contract and thus social security, paid leave and minimum-wage coverage.
insights.speaker: WILLIAM MALONEY
insights.so_what: Informality caps the formal tax/contribution base and consumer-credit depth across the region.
insights.quote: Today, roughly half of the region’s 325 million workers lack a formal labor contract

insights.claim: Informal self-employed owners of firms with fewer than five employees make up about 30% of Latin America's labor force and employ 85% of informal workers.
insights.speaker: WILLIAM MALONEY
insights.so_what: The micro-firm segment is where most informal labor sits, framing any formalization or productivity play.
insights.quote: they account for roughly 30% of the region’s labor force and employ 85% of informal workers

insights.claim: About 60% of Bolivia's workforce is self-employed, among the highest rates in the Western Hemisphere.
insights.speaker: WILLIAM MALONEY
insights.so_what: Bolivia is an extreme case of thin formal labor markets, limiting formal-sector-based growth and fiscal capacity.
insights.quote: Around 60% of its workforce is self-employed

insights.claim: The World Bank forecasts Latin America's GDP growth at 2.1% this year after 2.4% in 2025, and informality is thought to be both a symptom of distortions and a drag via low-productivity micro firms.
insights.speaker: WILLIAM MALONEY
insights.so_what: Decelerating, lackluster regional growth sets a low baseline for LatAm earnings and policy expectations.
insights.quote: the World Bank forecasts the region’s GDP will expand 2.1% this year after growing 2.4% in 2025

insights.claim: Self-employment falls consistently with income level, ranging from under 15% in advanced countries to 25-70% in Latin America and 90% in Africa, so Latin America is not pathologically high.
insights.speaker: WILLIAM MALONEY
insights.so_what: Challenges the narrative that informality itself is the region's core growth blocker.
insights.quote: Self-employment rates today range from under 15% in advanced countries to 90% in Africa to 25-70% in Latin America.

insights.claim: Argentina, Brazil, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Jamaica, Guatemala and Mexico sit on or below expected self-employment for their income, while Bolivia, Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Panama and Peru are substantially above.
insights.speaker: WILLIAM MALONEY
insights.so_what: Identifies which LatAm economies carry excess informality relative to development level.

insights.claim: Latin America's self-employment share today is roughly where Korea's and Japan's were at the same development level, and those countries still grew strongly.
insights.speaker: WILLIAM MALONEY
insights.so_what: High informality need not preclude rapid catch-up growth if other conditions are met.
insights.quote: Latin America and the Caribbean’s self-employment is more or less where Korea’s and Japan’s were at the same development level, and yet … they grew!

insights.claim: Over 70% of payroll workers in the Dominican Republic, Mexico and the Philippines say they would prefer self-employment, versus about 20% in Belgium, Finland and Norway.
insights.speaker: WILLIAM MALONEY
insights.so_what: Preference data implies informality is demand-driven by workers, so it will not unwind through enforcement alone.

insights.claim: The self-employed value amenities like flexibility, independence and being one's own boss at around 50% of actual earnings, while they value formal-sector benefits far below their cost.
insights.speaker: WILLIAM MALONEY
insights.so_what: Explains why formal jobs struggle to compete and why payroll-tax-heavy benefit systems push work off the books.
insights.quote: The self-employed report they value these amenities at around 50% of actual earnings while they value formal sector benefits far below their cost to workers and employers.

insights.claim: Micro firms with family employees and neighborhood clients have little reason to formalize because only the rare growth-oriented owner needs credit and state services.
insights.speaker: WILLIAM MALONEY
insights.so_what: Limits the addressable market for formal SME credit and fintech products aimed at micro firms.

insights.claim: Given workers' limited options, the region's large informal self-employed sector reflects rational choices and is in that sense normal, even optimal, despite being too large from a growth and social-protection perspective.
insights.speaker: WILLIAM MALONEY
insights.so_what: Reframes informality as an equilibrium outcome, implying slow change absent structural reform.

themes.theme: Policy levers that work and don't

insights.claim: Thirty percent of larger Latin American companies say they cannot grow for lack of qualified labor even as a vast pool of undereducated workers ends up in informal self-employment.
insights.speaker: WILLIAM MALONEY
insights.so_what: Skills scarcity is a binding constraint on scaling formal firms and on productivity.
insights.quote: 30% of bigger companies in the region report they can’t grow for lack of qualified labor

insights.claim: The region lacks high-quality 'transformational' entrepreneurs, so expanding quality tertiary education and entrepreneurial capabilities is needed to create formal jobs.
insights.speaker: WILLIAM MALONEY
insights.so_what: Supports investment cases in higher education and growth-stage entrepreneurship ecosystems.

insights.claim: World Bank B-READY indicators point to substantial business-climate distortions, with even large firms reporting inability to access credit to grow.
insights.speaker: WILLIAM MALONEY
insights.so_what: Credit constraints on large firms signal under-penetrated corporate lending opportunities and growth drag.
insights.quote: Even large firms report an inability to access credit to grow.

insights.claim: Moderate minimum-wage increases can raise earnings without job losses, but beyond a threshold they deter formal job creation and segment the labor market.
insights.speaker: WILLIAM MALONEY
insights.so_what: Aggressive minimum-wage hikes in LatAm should be read as formality-negative.
insights.quote: beyond a certain point, it deters formal job creation and segments the labor market

insights.claim: Workers value formal-sector benefits at about half their cost to society, and expanding universal (non-contributory) health and pension systems further lowers the implicit value of formality, pushing activity into informal micro firms.
insights.speaker: WILLIAM MALONEY
insights.so_what: Well-intended universal welfare expansions can shrink formal employment and contribution bases.
insights.quote: In most countries, workers value formal-sector benefits at about half their cost to society, which discourages formal job creation and incentivizes working off the books.

insights.claim: Programs that facilitate micro-firm formalization show disappointing results because these firms were not going to grow anyway; growth must come from a more entrepreneurial, innovative large-firm sector.
insights.speaker: WILLIAM MALONEY
insights.so_what: Discount policy announcements centered on micro-firm formalization; look to large-firm dynamism.
insights.quote: They weren’t going to grow anyway.

insights.claim: The policies most likely to reduce informality are those that do not target it directly: education overhaul, growth of medium and large formal firms, and integrated social-protection reform.
insights.speaker: WILLIAM MALONEY
insights.so_what: Signals where reform progress should be tracked to judge structural improvement in LatAm.
insights.quote: the policies required to reduce informality are those that don’t specifically target it
